title: #Love: Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi starrer Netflix new-age romance to premiere on October 2
author: Bollywood Hungama News Network
body:
Netflix is set to bring a contemporary take on romance with its upcoming Tamil series #Love, which will premiere on October 2. Produced by showrunner Soundarya Rajinikanth and directed by Balaji Mohan, the series stars Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi in a fresh on-screen pairing.
#Love: Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi starrer Netflix new-age romance to premiere on October 2
Set against the world of dating apps, #Love revolves around Tara and Matthew, two rival founders behind the dating platforms FOUND and Find My Bae. While the two have built businesses around helping people find love and compatibility, their own relationship is set to put their theories to the test.
The series explores the question of whether chemistry or compatibility ultimately matters more in a relationship, while also looking at how romance and connections have evolved in the age of dating apps, swipes, matches and unread messages.
Monika Shergill, Vice President, Content, Netflix India, said, “This has been a defining year for Netflix India, as we’ve deepened our investment in storytelling from the South of India — and #Love is a title we’re especially excited about. As we expand our slate across Tamil storytelling, this contemporary, feel-good rom com stood out as a genre and that was ready for a fresh, confident take. ##Love steps into that space with a modern, chemistry-driven love story about two rival dating-app founders who end up testing their own theories of love on each other. Director Balaji Mohan, together with showrunner and producer Soundarya Rajinikanth, brings a wonderfully playful perspective to the series, while Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi bring the central relationship to life with chemistry, warmth and humour. The series captures that giddy, unguarded feeling of falling for someone you never saw coming - funny, warm, and exhilarating to anyone who's ever overthought a text message.”
View this post on Instagram
 Speaking about the series, showrunner and producer Soundarya Rajinikanth said, "What drew me to #Love was how effortlessly it captures relationships today without losing its warmth and emotion. Balaji has created characters who are ambitious, flawed and incredibly easy to root for, and Arjun and Aishwarya bring such a refreshing energy to them. It's exactly the kind of contemporary story we were excited to bring to audiences with Netflix."
Director Balaji Mohan added, "When we made #Love, we wanted to tell a story that feels like it belongs to today. Romance has evolved, the way we meet people has changed, but the emotions at the heart of relationships remain incredibly familiar and timeless. What I love about this series is that it isn't only about two people falling for each other – friendship, family, ambition and finding yourself are equally important parts of their journeys."
#Love is written by Nirmal Williams, with Sharada Subramanian and Shweta Chakravarty serving as co-writers. The series is produced by May6 Entertainment Factory.
With Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi coming together for the first time in this pairing, #Love promises to explore modern romance through the lens of two people whose professional rivalry could lead to an unexpected personal connection.
#Love premieres October 2, only on Netflix.

title: I tried Co-star's Readme, the new dating app for readers
author: Chance Townsend
body:
Dating apps are in a weird place right now.
Culturally, people are starting to hate them. Whether out of personal distaste or for safety and privacy, more people want to return to the real world to find connections. But dating apps are still big business. Match Group reported net income of $613.5 million in 2025, up from $551.3 million in 2024 but down from $651.5 million in 2023. (Match Group owns Tinder, Hinge, and a slew of other dating apps.) So, despite the complaints, they're still making money, and a lot of it.
And the ecosystem is getting increasingly niche. There's an app for conservatives. For leftists. Farmers. Christians. Christian Farmers. The rich. The famous. People who like movies. Double daters. Freaks who use 4chan. And now, entering the field as of last week, the dating app for people who read.
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
Hearing that a dating app for readers now exists is, at this point, not novel. But what piqued my interest is that the app was being developed by Co-Star, the astrology app. Now that's novel. Beyond that, with the backing of the Co-Star brand and ecosystem, it commands interest among young adults who like astrology and are considered popular and fashionable, i.e., socialite New Yorkers and Brooklyn-based culture writers.
Readme is a book reader's dating app, and its mission is to match people spiritually, much like the classic "meet cute" at the bookstore. And maybe, just maybe, spark relationships where they don't have to expose their (male) partners for being illiterate.
It's a book-series-sized task from the Co-Star creators. However, from my brief experience with the app, I found it to be ambitious but not well-crafted enough to justify waiting for the next installment.
Getting started with Readme
Setting up an account is no different than any other app.
Users fill out their name, age, gender, dating preference, and what they're looking for. One of the app's two big hooks is that your queue of potential matches is built or can be filtered around your friends and people that are associated within two or three degrees of them. Kinda like old-school Hinge or Tinder's short-lived Friends of Friends feature.
Within the app, one of the filters lets you see only your friends, your friends' friends, or your friends' friends' friends. It's interesting in theory, in that Readme wants to replicate those meet-cute type moments that you read about in books. Not in practice, though, because none of my friends are on the app or know it exists. It just launched, after all. But maybe this is my sign to start hosting more parties.
The other big hook is the quiz that "uses psycholinguistics to explore the hidden links between how you read and how you relate," according to the app. It's 25 questions, with the bulk asking you to pick which of two quotes you like or dislike the least. After you pick, it reveals which author it was.
For example, some of the authors I got were Henry Miller, Robert Frost, Casey McQuiston (of Red, White, & Royal Blue fame), and Jonathan Safran Foer. The latter was personally embarassing cause I really, really dislike Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close, as a book and a movie.
Between the quotes are questions about your political beliefs, communication style, and the genres of books you like to read. The latter was particularly irritating because much of the copy in the app has millennial-esque snark that tries to be "smashpunk" but is just grating. I like reading historical non-fiction, and the closest option to that was "straight up facts." Another genre option was "the writing on the wall," which is so eye-rolling. Obviously, these are my own personal misgivings, but Readme somehow tries too hard not to be like the other apps, yet also wants you to know it's cool, hip, and too irony-pilled to be authentic.
At the end of the day, language like that is fine, but seeing "communism will win" and "nostalgic for Barack Obama" as options under "political beliefs" did get a laugh out of me.
Something not included in the questionnaire, or seemingly anywhere on Readme, is astrological signs. Nowhere to put my birthdate, time, and place. So if you're looking for astrological compatability, Readme isn't it. (Yet?)
After the questionnaire, you get a report on what your language preferences "reveal about who you are and how you love."
I got "Former Gifted Child" because I prefer metonymy over metaphor. The app's way of telling me I lack imagination. "You rely on structures and systems to make sense of the world," the app tells me. I wouldn't say it's wrong, because my parents always believed I was a precocious kid. Turns out I had ADHD the whole time, so maybe the app was onto something.
The report also details How I Love and What You Need. Overall, the report is neat but a bit basic if you remove the flowery language. I like the book recommendations it gave me, and it even gave me some questions I should ask on a first date. Per my ReadMe report, I'm a lover boy at heart and need someone who's not as rigid.
"You need someone who finds the social script so uninteresting that they haven't bothered reading it, and don't know or care whether they're following or breaking it," my report read. Sometimes it's hard to tell whether the copy was written by a millennial ad executive or by ChatGPT's poor interpretation of one.
Using the Readme app
So now that the setup is done, what's the actual app like? It's....fine. It's definitely a dating app. You click the heart to like and the minus sign to dislike. At the bottom of every profile, you'll see a similarity score based on their quiz answers and choices. And that's it, honestly.
The big glaring issue here is that Readme just doesn't have the juice yet.
Immediately upon getting to the app proper, my recommended likes all live in New York. I live in Chicago. There's no filter or setting for distance. The only settings you can change are age, gender, and mutuals. For me, the app is a nonstarter. Not that it can't be successful, but I live in the third-largest city in the U.S., and Readme's algorithm is only showing me people who don't live in my city. Maybe it should've had a limited launch in Brooklyn first, gotten some hype, and then rolled out to other major cities.
I swiped right on between 70 and 80 profiles in my selected age range (24-32) before running out of people to see. None of them was based in Chicago. I saw accounts from Vermont, New Jersey, Denver, San Francisco, and even Tokyo. But not one in 70+ swipes lived in Chicago or set their location as Chicago.
I guess on the positive side, unlike the big power players like Hinge and Tinder, you do have unlimited likes. It'll be interesting to see if that'll be the case as the app gets more attention — venture capital and vibes can only subsidize an app for so long. Maybe then the dating pool will keep me invested enough not to be on the app when the bill comes due.
To be frank, having a cis hetero male perspective on the dating app for readers probably doesn't give one a sense of what the dating pool is like. Statistically, people don't read that much in general, but women read far more often than men. According to a Pew Research Center study conducted in Oct. 2025, "women are more likely than men to say they've read a book in the past 12 months."
One can extrapolate from the many cultural reasons why women read more than men. I imagine the main appeal of an app like Readme for women is that avid reading can be seen as a sign of intelligence, empathy, and curiosity. With the rise of dudebro, Barstool conservatism in young men, an online dating app that, to an extent, filters one from an embarrassing partner, is appealing.
All of that said, this is from my perspective as a 28-year-old Black man living in Chicago. The aesthetic leanings of Readme's dating pool are what you'd expect from an app that markets itself as a zine-style, indie sleaze, Y2K vintage fashion store you'd find in the more affluent parts of Brooklyn. In short, it's very white. Which is not bad, and I don't mean to imply that there aren't women of color on the app, but as it's been researched before, dating apps' algorithms are not kind to Black women, or people of color in general.
It's a shame because its style and interface are easy to get acclimated with, but beyond the mutuals feature and the quiz, it doesn't really do enough to stand out. If anything, what sets Readme apart from the crowd of hyper-niche dating apps is that it knows and markets itself exactly towards the audience it wants.
That's fine, but it'd be interesting to see whether it can expand beyond that — if it even wants to.
Chance Townsend is the General Assignments Editor at Mashable, covering tech, video games, dating apps, digital culture, and whatever else comes his way. He has a Master's in Journalism from the University of North Texas and is a proud orange cat father. His writing has also appeared in PC Mag and Mother Jones.

title: #Love OTT release date and platform announced: When and where to watch Aishwarya Lekshmi and Arjun Das’s Tamil modern romance series
author: Sushmita Dey; ET Entertainment Desk
body:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Streaming details of Tamil series #Love
#Love will premiere on Netflix on October 2, 2026. The series will be available in Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, giving viewers across multiple South Indian language markets a chance to watch the new romantic drama.
At the centre of #Love is a question that has become increasingly relevant in the world of modern dating, should people look for chemistry or compatibility when choosing a partner?
The series uses the dating-app world to explore this debate. Its story follows characters who have their own ideas about what makes a relationship work. While chemistry can create an immediate connection between two people, compatibility may determine whether that relationship can survive in the long run.
Aishwarya Lekshmi plays a single dating-app CEO
Aishwarya Lekshmi plays Tara, a woman who runs a dating app but is single herself. Her professional life revolves around helping people find potential partners, but her personal life does not appear to follow the same formula.
Arjun Das plays the other central character. In the latest glimpse, his character questions Tara about her belief that compatibility is enough for a successful relationship. Tara argues that if two people are genuinely compatible, chemistry will eventually follow. Their exchange sets up the central debate of the series while also giving the romance a light and conversational tone.
The new pairing of Aishwarya Lekshmi and Arjun Das is another major attraction.
More about #Love
#Love is directed by filmmaker Balaji Mohan, known for his work in Tamil cinema. The series is showrun and produced by Soundarya Rajinikanth, daughter of superstar Rajinikanth.
The series is produced by May6 Entertainment Factory. It is written by Nirmal Williams, with Sharada Subramanian and Shweta Chakravarty serving as co-writers.
The makers announced #Love earlier this year as part of Netflix India’s slate of upcoming releases for 2026. Along with the announcement, the streaming platform released a teaser that introduced the dating-app setting and the romantic conflict at the centre of the story.
The latest announcement has now confirmed the release date and languages. For Aishwarya Lekshmi, #Love marks an important career milestone as her digital debut. The actress has worked across Malayalam and Tamil cinema.
Arjun Das, meanwhile, joins her in what looks like a different kind of romantic pairing for both actors. The series uses their characters’ differing opinions about love to build its central conflict.
#Love premieres October 2, 2026, on Netflix. The series will stream in Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. Stay tuned!

title: Offset Sets Up Faux Relationship Advice Hotline NEED FM to Promote New Single
author: Jose Martinez
body:
Key Takeaways
- Offset launched a faux late-night advice hotline called "NEED FM" on Tuesday, Sept. 15, giving out the number (470) 742-6949, ostensibly for fans to call with relationship problems.
- The hotline actually promotes Offset's new single "Something I Need,” which drops Friday, Sept. 18.
Offset will be taking your calls — sort of.
In an Instagram post shared on Tuesday (Sep. 15), the rapper announced the launch of NEED FM, which appeared to be a late-night advice hotline for anyone in need of answers.
The post is accompanied by a phone number, 470-742-6949. However, a call will not lead to a chance to have a conversation with Offset about your love life. Instead, it will trigger a text message with a pre-save link for his upcoming single “Something I Need.”
While a new single from Offset is on the horizon, Quavo recently confirmed the two will reunite for a final Migos album and tour.
"We coming back," Quavo told DJ Greg Street on the Atlanta radio station V-103. "We're going to do it one more time."
It’s uncertain if this new Migos album will feature posthumous contributions from Takeoff, who fatally shot in Houston four years ago.
The announcement of a new Migos album comes months after Quavo posted a photo of himself and Takeoff and hinted at a reunion, writing, “AINT NO NEW CHAPTER JUST THE NEXT ONE!!!”
Offset followed up with a photo of the trio around the time of 2021’s Culture III, with the caption, “On dat!!!!”
Following the release of Culture III, tensions between Offset and Quavo caused them to part ways. The two set their differences aside and took the stage together for a tribute to Takeoff at the 2023 BET Awards.
Offset indicated on 7PM in Brooklyn With Carmelo Anthony that he and Quavo were in a better place and were speaking somewhat regularly.

title: Elena e il love bombing: “Mi ha ricoperto di attenzioni, per poi farmi sentire sbagliata in tutto”
author: Veronica Mazza
body:
"Cara redazione, mi chiamo Elena P. e vi scrivo da Bologna, la città dove sono nata, cresciuta e dove da quattro anni lavoro in uno studio di architettura. Ho 29 anni e sono sempre stata una persona razionale, con i piedi ben piantati per terra. Non ho mai creduto ai colpi di fulmine cinematografici o ai grandi gesti eclatanti, almeno fino a quando, a un'inaugurazione di una mostra, non ho conosciuto Marco, 32 anni, designer d'interni.
Il primo mese assieme è stato.. come dire? Una tempesta meravigliosa. Il rapporto cresceva con un’intensità che non avevo mai provato in vita mia. Marco mi cercava a qualsiasi ora, mi mandava messaggi bellissimi prima ancora che mi svegliassi. Nel giro di due settimane sapeva tutto di me. Dopo tre, mi ha fatto recapitare un mazzo di tulipani enormi direttamente in studio, con un biglietto che diceva: 'Per la donna che mi ha cambiato la prospettiva'. I miei colleghi sorridevano, io mi sentivo al centro del mondo.
Ha voluto bruciare i tempi: mi ha presentato ai suoi amici storici, mi ha portato nei suoi posti del cuore e, dopo appena un mese e mezzo, durante un weekend sulle colline marchigiane, ha iniziato a parlare di convivenza. Mi diceva che non aveva mai sentito una connessione simile, che ero l'altra metà della mela che aspettava da sempre. Mi sembrava un sogno. E proprio perché sembrava un sogno, ho abbassato tutte le mie difese”.
Se vuoi mandare la tua storia, per vederla pubblicata, scrivi una e-mail a: maldamore@repubblica.it
Il cambio di rotta, improvviso
"Il crollo è arrivato al compimento del secondo mese, da un giorno all'altro, senza che ci fosse mai stato un litigio, una discussione o un motivo apparente. Ricordo benissimo quella serata. Eravamo a cena e Marco, inspiegabilmente, era silenzioso, distante. Alla mia domanda se andasse tutto bene, mi ha risposto con un tono gelido, mai sentito prima: 'Sì, solo che a volte parli davvero troppo. Sembri sempre così ansiosa di riempire i silenzi'. Sono rimasta pietrificata. Solo una settimana prima mi diceva che adorava la mia parlantina e la mia energia. Da quel momento in poi, la persona adorante dei primi due mesi è letteralmente scomparsa. Al suo posto c'era un uomo critico, freddo, imprevedibile. I messaggi sono diventati telegrafici e diradati. I fiori sono spariti, così come i discorsi sul futuro. Se proponevo di vederci, sbuffava: 'Elena, sei troppo appiccicosa, hai un bisogno continuo di conferme. Mi soffochi'. Se provavo a spiegargli come mi sentivo, ribaltava la situazione facendo passare me per paranoica, pesante o emotivamente instabile”.
La dipendenza dal 'primo Marco'
"La cosa peggiore di questa dinamica, che solo dopo ho capito essere love bombing seguito da svalutazione, è il corto circuito psicologico che ti crea in testa. Entri in una forma di dipendenza pura: passi le giornate a chiederti cosa hai fatto di sbagliato per far svanire quel ragazzo meraviglioso dell'inizio. Finisci per colpevolizzarti, pensi che se sarai più docile, più silenziosa o più accomodante, lui tornerà a guardarti come prima. Ero arrivata al punto di camminare sulle uova. Ogni messaggio che gli inviavo lo rileggevo dieci volte per paura di 'infastidirlo'. Ma più cercavo di compiacerlo, più lui mi trattava con distacco e disprezzo. Un giorno, dopo che l'ennesimo appuntamento programmato è stato cancellato con un laconico 'Ho da fare, non fare la drammatica', sono scoppiata a piangere nel bagno del mio studio, disperandomi sul perché l’uomo che diceva di amarmi mi trattasse come se fossi niente. Ci sono voluti mesi di lacrime per capire che il 'Marco innamorato' del primo mese non era la sua vera natura, ma solo un'esca. La vera persona era quella fredda e manipolatoria emersa dopo. Ero sfortunatamente incappata in un narcisista, che usava quella dinamica per intortare la sua preda e una volta agganciata trattarla come una pezza da piedi. Per questo ho deciso di chiudere io, bloccandolo ovunque per evitare che tornasse con un altro ciclo di promesse quando si fosse sentito solo. Non è stato facile e la ferita resta: come si fa a fidarsi di nuovo di qualcuno dopo che ti hanno fatto credere di essere l'amore della loro vita, per poi trattarti come una scocciatura qualunque?”
La psicologa: “Attenzione alle manifestazioni eclatanti di affetto, creano dipendenza affettiva”
“La storia di Elena mette in luce un fenomeno relazionale complesso e doloroso: il love bombing, una dinamica frequentemente osservata nelle relazioni con persone che presentano tratti narcisistici. Si tratta di un comportamento caratterizzato da manifestazioni eclatanti di affetto, attenzioni e promesse che, anziché favorire una conoscenza graduale dell’altro, accelerano il coinvolgimento emotivo e creano le basi per una successiva dipendenza affettiva”, spiega la dott.ssa Anna Merolle, psicologa, psicoterapeuta ed esperta di dinamiche relazionali. “Come racconta Elena, messaggi continui, regali, dichiarazioni intense e progetti di vita condivisi in tempi molto rapidi possono dare l’impressione di aver trovato un amore straordinario. In realtà, questa intensa idealizzazione può rendere la persona più vulnerabile e più incline, in seguito, a giustificare comportamenti incoerenti o manipolatori.
Nella storia di Elena il vero punto di svolta non sono i tulipani o le dichiarazioni d’amore, ma il cambiamento improvviso. Nel giro di pochi giorni, la donna che veniva esaltata diventa “troppo ansiosa”, “troppo appiccicosa”, “troppo pesante”. È il passaggio dall’idealizzazione alla svalutazione: il partner affettuoso lascia spazio a una persona fredda, critica e distante. Questo cambiamento genera un forte disorientamento psicologico, perché la vittima continua a confrontare il partner del presente con quello dell’inizio, cercando disperatamente di farlo tornare.
Da quel momento si entra in un circolo vizioso. Invece di chiedersi perché l’altro sia cambiato, ci si domanda cosa ci sia di sbagliato in sé. Si controllano le parole, si evitano i conflitti, si mettono da parte i propri bisogni nel tentativo di recuperare l’affetto perduto. Così l’autostima si indebolisce e si perde progressivamente di vista se stessi.
Elena descrive con lucidità la dipendenza dal “primo Marco”, cioè dall’immagine del partner idealizzato conosciuto all’inizio della relazione. È un vero e proprio cortocircuito psicologico: ci si aggrappa ai ricordi dei momenti felici nella speranza che quella versione dell’altro possa tornare. Ed è proprio questa speranza a rendere così difficile interrompere la relazione.
La decisione di Elena di chiudere ogni contatto rappresenta un importante atto di tutela personale. Uscire da una relazione caratterizzata da queste dinamiche significa iniziare un percorso di recupero della propria identità e della fiducia in se stessi. In molti casi, un percorso psicoterapeutico può aiutare a elaborare l’esperienza e ricostruire il proprio valore.
L’insegnamento più importante che emerge dalla vicenda di Elena è che l’amore autentico può essere intenso, ma è soprattutto coerente. Non costringe a rincorrere continuamente la versione migliore dell’altro, né fa sentire speciali un giorno e inadeguati quello successivo. Quando una relazione porta a dubitare costantemente del proprio valore e a vivere nell’incertezza, è proprio la sua instabilità a renderla pericolosa. Perché l’amore non si misura dalla forza dell’entusiasmo iniziale, ma dalla capacità di rimanere coerente, rispettoso e affidabile nel tempo”.

rss_title: Elena and love bombing: "It covered me with attention, and then made me feel wrong in everything"
rss_body:
"Cara redazione, mi chiamo Elena P. e vi scrivo da Bologna, la città dove sono nata, cresciuta e dove da quattro anni lavoro in uno studio di architettura. Ho 29 anni e sono sempre stata una persona razionale, con i piedi ben piantati per terra. Non ho mai creduto ai colpi di fulmine cinematografici o ai grandi gesti eclatanti, almeno fino a quando, a un'inaugurazione di una mostra, non ho conosciuto Marco, 32 anni, designer d'interni.

Il primo mese assieme è stato.. come dire? Una tempesta meravigliosa. Il rapporto cresceva con un’intensità che non avevo mai provato in vita mia. Marco mi cercava a qualsiasi ora, mi mandava messaggi bellissimi prima ancora che mi svegliassi. Nel giro di due settimane sapeva tutto di me. Dopo tre, mi ha fatto recapitare un mazzo di tulipani enormi direttamente in studio, con un biglietto che diceva: 'Per la donna che mi ha cambiato la prospettiva'. I miei colleghi sorridevano, io mi sentivo al centro del mondo.

Ha voluto bruciare i tempi: mi ha presentato ai suoi amici storici, mi ha portato nei suoi posti del cuore e, dopo appena un mese e mezzo, durante un weekend sulle colline marchigiane, ha iniziato a parlare di convivenza. Mi diceva che non aveva mai sentito una connessione simile, che ero l'altra metà della mela che aspettava da sempre. Mi sembrava un sogno. E proprio perché sembrava un sogno, ho abbassato tutte le mie difese”.

Se vuoi mandare la tua storia, per vederla pubblicata, scrivi una e-mail a: maldamore@repubblica.it

Il cambio di rotta, improvviso

"Il crollo è arrivato al compimento del secondo mese, da un giorno all'altro, senza che ci fosse mai stato un litigio, una discussione o un motivo apparente. Ricordo benissimo quella serata. Eravamo a cena e Marco, inspiegabilmente, era silenzioso, distante. Alla mia domanda se andasse tutto bene, mi ha risposto con un tono gelido, mai sentito prima: 'Sì, solo che a volte parli davvero troppo. Sembri sempre così ansiosa di riempire i silenzi'. Sono rimasta pietrificata. Solo una settimana prima mi diceva che adorava la mia parlantina e la mia energia. Da quel momento in poi, la persona adorante dei primi due mesi è letteralmente scomparsa. Al suo posto c'era un uomo critico, freddo, imprevedibile. I messaggi sono diventati telegrafici e diradati. I fiori sono spariti, così come i discorsi sul futuro. Se proponevo di vederci, sbuffava: 'Elena, sei troppo appiccicosa, hai un bisogno continuo di conferme. Mi soffochi'. Se provavo a spiegargli come mi sentivo, ribaltava la situazione facendo passare me per paranoica, pesante o emotivamente instabile”.

La dipendenza dal 'primo Marco'

"La cosa peggiore di questa dinamica, che solo dopo ho capito essere love bombing seguito da svalutazione, è il corto circuito psicologico che ti crea in testa. Entri in una forma di dipendenza pura: passi le giornate a chiederti cosa hai fatto di sbagliato per far svanire quel ragazzo meraviglioso dell'inizio. Finisci per colpevolizzarti, pensi che se sarai più docile, più silenziosa o più accomodante, lui tornerà a guardarti come prima. Ero arrivata al punto di camminare sulle uova. Ogni messaggio che gli inviavo lo rileggevo dieci volte per paura di 'infastidirlo'. Ma più cercavo di compiacerlo, più lui mi trattava con distacco e disprezzo. Un giorno, dopo che l'ennesimo appuntamento programmato è stato cancellato con un laconico 'Ho da fare, non fare la drammatica', sono scoppiata a piangere nel bagno del mio studio, disperandomi sul perché l’uomo che diceva di amarmi mi trattasse come se fossi niente. Ci sono voluti mesi di lacrime per capire che il 'Marco innamorato' del primo mese non era la sua vera natura, ma solo un'esca. La vera persona era quella fredda e manipolatoria emersa dopo. Ero sfortunatamente incappata in un narcisista, che usava quella dinamica per intortare la sua preda e una volta agganciata trattarla come una pezza da piedi. Per questo ho deciso di chiudere io, bloccandolo ovunque per evitare che tornasse con un altro ciclo di promesse quando si fosse sentito solo. Non è stato facile e la ferita resta: come si fa a fidarsi di nuovo di qualcuno dopo che ti hanno fatto credere di essere l'amore della loro vita, per poi trattarti come una scocciatura qualunque?”

title: C.D. Leganés and La Joya renew their sponsorship agreement - C.D. Leganés - Official Website
body:
C.D. Leganés and La Joya have reached an agreement to renew their sponsorship partnership for the 2026–27 season, thereby strengthening a relationship based on mutual trust and a commitment to the club.
Thanks to this agreement, La Joya will continue to be part of the C.D. Leganés family as the club’s official sponsor during the current season, maintaining a prominent presence at Ontime Butarque Stadium and in various initiatives organized by the club.
Among the initiatives included in this renewal, La Joya will have advertising space on the stadium’s LED screens during first-team matches at Ontime Butarque. Additionally, it will continue to provide a ham-carving service in the VIP box, adding value to the experience of the club’s guests and partners on every match day.
A partnership that will extend to various events organized by the club
The partnership will also extend to various events organized by C.D. Leganés throughout the season, strengthening the brand’s visibility and its connection with the “Pepinera” fan base. Similarly, both organizations will work together on new initiatives set to launch soon within the club’s Fan Zone.
C.D. Leganés President Eduardo Cosín stated that they are “very happy to once again have La Joya on board; they are part of the family that supports us day in and day out. They seek moments and experiences, and we share the desire to bring joy and spend time together—and doing so for another year with them is a source of joy for us.”
The partnership aims to continue creating valuable experiences for fans
For his part, José Quintana, La Joya’s ambassador, said he was “very happy to be here for the second consecutive year. This year gives us the opportunity to continue participating in events and reaching a young audience, and we’re very happy to be able to continue for another year.”
With this renewal, C.D. Leganés and La Joya are solidifying a partnership that will continue to grow throughout the 2026–27 season, with the goal of continuing to create meaningful experiences for fans, sponsors, and members of the blue-and-white family.

title: Former MP Evelyn Anite warns against dishonesty in long-distance romance
author: Benjie
body:
Hon. Evelyn Anite has shared tips on how couples can successfully maintain long-distance relationships, revealing that she is currently in one herself.
Taking to her TikTok, the former Member of Parliament for Koboko Municipality explained that communication and consistency are some of the most important things couples need to keep their relationships strong when they are separated by distance.
She advised partners to make it a habit to communicate every day, including sending a message to their loved one in the morning after waking up and another at night before going to bed.
“Communicate. You have to always be transparent and communicate with your partner,” she advised, emphasizing the importance of staying in touch despite the physical distance.
According to her, couples in long-distance relationships should make an effort to remain present in each other’s lives because a lack of communication can create room for disconnection.
When you’re not in touch, out of mind is out of sight.
She also acknowledged that there are many attractive people who could potentially come into a relationship, but believes maintaining regular communication can help couples remain connected and committed to each other.
There are so many beautiful and good-looking people out there who are willing to snatch your partner, but if you keep in touch with them, they don’t get a chance to even think about other people.
Hon. Anite further cautioned couples against dishonesty, noting that trust is another important foundation for making a long-distance relationship work.
“Do not tell lies, because if you do, you’ll lose them,” she said.

title: Claire-Louise Bennett: 'Difference, chance and risk should be at the heart of the experience of love, something almost impossible in a world of dating apps'
author: Laura Fernández
body:
Claire-Louise Bennett has said she is fascinated by the ways we exist in other people’s minds, by what we become when we are reduced to an idea. Perhaps that is why her fiction is always filtered through a consciousness: someone obsessively searching for a way out, or for a place in the world. Is love a kind of compass? Can it give shape to the self, each time in a different way?
Bennett thinks it should, but she also believes we are increasingly preventing it from doing so. Dating apps are no help, she says. In her latest novel, the intense, labyrinthine and deeply interior Big Kiss, Bye-Bye, she asks how love places us before a mirror and reveals the parts of ourselves we would never admit are also there. And something like that can only be reached, as Anaïs Nin might have put it, through the mystery of what draws us to another person when nothing has been agreed in advance.
At her home in Galway, Ireland, Bennett, who is also the author of Checkout 19 and Pond, answers the video call. She is seated at an enormous table. It is covered with notebooks and crystal spheres. Nearby, she says, there is even a glass penguin. And the mug from which she occasionally takes a sip still contains some of the Yogi Choco tea she made for herself a little while ago.
Question. Big Kiss, Bye-Bye is a long conversation between two lovers that recalls both the obsessive prose of Thomas Bernhard and the stream of consciousness of Virginia Woolf. In that conversation, Xavier functions as a kind of totem, a looming presence against which the narrator defines herself, sketching an outline of who she is and making herself real. To what extent is love a kind of existential compass?
Answer. I love the image. Yes. Without a doubt, it is. I deeply believe that love is an existential experience. I read Alain Badiou’s In Praise of Love a long time ago and felt he was right about everything. At the center of the experience of love should be difference, chance and risk — elements that today, in a world dominated by app-mediated dating, are practically impossible. Today’s world encourages us to think in terms of compatibility. We look for someone who fits us, who reaffirms who we already are. That very conscious way of approaching relationships can be quite transactional, like shopping, because it forces us to define in advance what we are looking for in a partner, what we expect from a relationship and what our limits are. Love is the opposite. Love is the great revealer.
Q. In what sense?
A. Love reveals who we really are. It shows us things about ourselves we would never have dared to imagine, much less admit. That is why attraction that arises in real life has such enormous force and, at the same time, is so unsettling. Anaïs Nin was terrified of being fixed into a stable, defined personality. She wanted to flow, to be always transforming, and for her love, made that perpetual motion possible — that existential expansion. Her stories and novels show how intimate encounters can uproot you, turn your world upside down, take you far from whoever you think you are at that moment. What today might be dismissed as mere romanticism is, in reality, what makes love a deeply singular experience. After all, it is the most powerful force there is, provided one has the courage not to try to manage or direct it.
Q. In your case, writing itself also seems to function as a compass, a way of finding your path through words and through what words construct: fragmentary scenes, memories seen from a single perspective, disorientation, something mutable and therefore open to transformation. Would you say that’s true? What are we, really? Everything we might yet become, or everything we have been?
A. Sometimes I feel I do not have a self, at least not in a strict sense. What I am is a place where very diverse forces orbit — and sometimes conflict —: archetypes, psychic patterns, impulses and memories both personal and collective, and many other things. There is a huge part of what I am that is completely unknown to me. And yet I know those unknown elements exert a huge influence on my everyday life. It is tempting to use writing as a way to make sense of that chaos and learn to navigate it, but the satisfaction it offers is only superficial. That is not what I am looking for. Samuel Beckett said the artist’s task is not to clarify things, but to find a way to make room for disorder. I completely agree.
Q. Is that why your writing has this quality of being unreliable, of constantly transforming itself?
A. Yes. My writing follows a winding path, full of false starts, dead ends, and overgrown landscapes. And, every now and then, small clearings appear where there is a sense of respite, immediacy, and communion. The thing is, I don’t write to affirm anything. I write by denying, subverting, and undermining. And that’s because, although we need to place some faith in reality in order to keep on living, deep down I don’t believe that what we call reality actually exists.

I write by denying, subverting, and undermining. rss_title: Claire-Louise Bennett: 'Difference, chance and risk should be at the heart of the experience of love, something almost impossible in a world of dating apps'
rss_body:
Claire-Louise Bennett has said she is fascinated by the ways we exist in other people’s minds, by what we become when we are reduced to an idea. Perhaps that is why her fiction is always filtered through a consciousness: someone obsessively searching for a way out, or for a place in the world. Is love a kind of compass? Can it give shape to the self, each time in a different way?
Bennett thinks it should, but she also believes we are increasingly preventing it from doing so. Dating apps are no help, she says. In her latest novel, the intense, labyrinthine and deeply interior Big Kiss, Bye-Bye, she asks how love places us before a mirror and reveals the parts of ourselves we would never admit are also there. And something like that can only be reached, as Anaïs Nin might have put it, through the mystery of what draws us to another person when nothing has been agreed in advance.
At her home in Galway, Ireland, Bennett, who is also the author of Checkout 19 and Pond, answers the video call. She is seated at an enormous table. It is covered with notebooks and crystal spheres. Nearby, she says, there is even a glass penguin. And the mug from which she occasionally takes a sip still contains some of the Yogi Choco tea she made for herself a little while ago.
Question. Big Kiss, Bye-Bye is a long conversation between two lovers that recalls both the obsessive prose of Thomas Bernhard and the stream of consciousness of Virginia Woolf. In that conversation, Xavier functions as a kind of totem, a looming presence against which the narrator defines herself, sketching an outline of who she is and making herself real. To what extent is love a kind of existential compass?
Answer. I love the image. Yes. Without a doubt, it is. I deeply believe that love is an existential experience. I read Alain Badiou’s In Praise of Love a long time ago and felt he was right about everything. Today’s world encourages us to think in terms of compatibility. We look for someone who fits us, who reaffirms who we already are. That very conscious way of approaching relationships can be quite transactional, like shopping, because it forces us to define in advance what we are looking for in a partner, what we expect from a relationship and what our limits are. Love is the opposite. Love is the great revealer.

title: I Don’t Want to Live In a World Where Ted Lasso Is on Dating Apps
author: Eric Francisco
body:
You won’t see a more concentrated instance of how funny and frustrating Ted Lasso can be at the same time than an overly long bit where Ted fills out his dating profile. In signature Lasso fashion, mundane questions are but prompts for Ted to run wild with his brand of mistaken yet sincere and wholesome wit. (And what a way to target me, personally, with references to Stephen Sondheim’s Company and David Fincher’s Zodiac.) It’s cute, mostly, until it gets embarrassing. I fail to find a more apt summary for Ted Lasso as a whole.
In the seventh episode of season 4, “Yes & Baby,” we finally take a closer look into the lives of the Lady Greyhounds. It’s a safe assumption that playing second division women’s football doesn’t match up to Premier League paydays, but the series makes a legitimate effort to show what, exactly, all the women have to lose if they don’t shape up and get butts into stadium seats fast enough. Meanwhile, Rebecca and the Richmond front office navigate the uglier sides of the football business as Dani Rojas’s scummy agent tries some underhanded negotiating. Coach Alice (Tanya Reynolds), now in the new year, learns the power of “yes,” while Roy Kent’s love life hits a serious juncture.
Then, there’s Ted. He has permission to date now, which he always had and didn’t need, but it’s meaningful to have the door open for him. But it’s been a while since Ted put himself out there. And have you heard? Dating sucks now. Sucks! Vox’s Today, Explained just did a whole episode about it. Ted’s walking back into the jungles after a lifetime of domesticity, and he’s frozen stiff by a questionnaire.
I don’t blame him. Imagine being Ted, a grown man on the other side of a decade-plus-long marriage with a kid in high school. Being asked to describe oneself in three words must be banal, mortifying, and not the least bit embarrassing. Which is why I appreciate the resolution the episode offers to Ted, and perhaps all of us in the trenches of apps and endless first dates. Before we can commit ourselves to someone else, it’s critical that we recognize our own worth and love ourselves first.
What a beautiful sentiment. If only the rest of Ted Lasso were as brilliant and graceful.
“Yes & Baby” is hardly a stinker—I’d even wager to say it’s a rather good episode—but it’s just another episode where Ted Lasso’s forward progress feels perpetually hindered by its umpteenth step on a rake. I was on board for so much of it. Really. Rebecca, Zelda, and Leslie’s cartoonish phone call had me in stitches (I need Zelda’s “KAHK-sacker” as a text alert), and the farewell between Roy and Dr. Beaumont (Laura Haddock) was genuinely moving. The latter reminded me how, after watching an early cut of Spider-Man 2, Chris Carrabba of Dashboard Confessional wrote “Vindicated,” a song centered on the significance of recognizing someone else. (“I am seeing in me now the things you swore you saw yourself.”) How apt the song plays in the end credits after Peter and MJ decide on a life together, no secrets or masks between them. No, Roy and Dr. Erin don’t capital-L love each other in the same way, but there’s genuine power still in telling someone that you see them.
I’m not even mad at the convenient resolution over the “Believe” sign subplot either. When the team sees Coach Alice taping Ted’s new sign in their locker room, they’re swift to a deep and callous cynicism that even Ted Lasso’s folksy superpowers seem powerless to fix. But all it takes is Lizzie’s adorable four-year-old to read it aloud and they’re suddenly motivated to, well, “believe.” (And win.) Their transformation comes from nowhere and it’s all very tonally maudlin—which is, let’s be real here, typical Ted Lasso—but it’s got enough of the show’s missing season 1 magic to sweep me away.
Which is why I am irritated that the show habitually resorts to eye-rolling zingers and punchlines. The whole two-minute stretch where Keeley helps Ted fill his profile runs the gamut of cringe to funny to embarrassing to impressive to cringe again. (And to not even play The Greatest American Hero theme over the end credits? Come on! Whack!)
I like fun and whimsy too. And I can appreciate Jason Sudeikis’s karaoke pipes. But having your middle-aged protagonist swear he’s “invited to the cookout” and is pro-pronouns... Man, it’s just exhausting for what is ultimately just a ninety-second gag. Nothing about this sinks Ted Lasso completely. But it’s discouraging how the show can be capable of wisdom and grace only to zap the air out of the room with weak grasps for—I’ll say it, I don’t care—woke points. At the end of the episode, Ted himself finds the three words to describe himself: “I am lovable.” That’s beautiful. That works. It’s amazing how little can go a long way.

title: Love bombing, Messina tra le città italiane più colpite: lo ha vissuto il 24% dei messinesi
author: Redazione
body:
C'è chi all'inizio di una frequentazione viene travolto da attenzioni, messaggi, complimenti e dimostrazioni d'affetto. Poi, improvvisamente, qualcosa cambia: quelle attenzioni si riducono o scompaiono. È il "love bombing", una delle dinamiche analizzate in una nuova ricerca di Unobravo sul modo in cui gli italiani vivono il dating contemporaneo. E Messina spicca tra le città prese in esame.
Secondo i dati diffusi dalla società di psicologia online, il 24% dei messinesi dichiara di aver vissuto un'esperienza riconducibile al love bombing. Una percentuale che colloca la città al terzo posto tra quelle analizzate, alle spalle di Reggio Emilia, con il 28%, e Verona, con il 25%. Seguono Modena e Palermo, entrambe al 23%.
Il dato messinese risulta superiore alla media nazionale, che si attesta al 16%. La ricerca, realizzata su un campione rappresentativo di 1.670 adulti italiani, ha preso in esame diversi comportamenti associati alle relazioni e alle frequentazioni contemporanee, cercando di capire quanto siano diffusi e quale impatto abbiano sulle persone.
Situationship, slow fading e ghosting
Il love bombing è soltanto una delle dinamiche considerate dallo studio. Si tratta di una strategia di manipolazione psicologica in cui una persona ricopre l'altra di attenzioni, affetto, lodi e promesse esagerate fin dall'inizio di una relazione, con l'obiettivo nascosto di ottenere potere e controllo.
A livello nazionale, il fenomeno più citato è però quello delle situationship, ovvero relazioni dai confini poco definiti, riferite dal 20% degli intervistati. Seguono lo slow fading, caratterizzato da una progressiva riduzione della comunicazione, al 19%, e ghosting e segnali contraddittori, entrambi al 18%.
Il love bombing si ferma invece al 16%, mentre il breadcrumbing, cioè il mantenimento di contatti sporadici e poco coinvolgenti, riguarda il 14% del campione. Più contenute le percentuali relative a benching, orbiting e zombieing, tutte al 10%. Nel complesso, il 34% degli intervistati afferma di non aver sperimentato nessuno dei comportamenti presi in considerazione.
Per metà degli italiani il dating è difficile da interpretare
La ricerca fotografa un rapporto non sempre semplice con le nuove modalità di frequentazione. Il 51% degli italiani dichiara di trovare il dating moderno difficile da interpretare o poco chiaro, mentre il 66% considera comuni o molto comuni comportamenti come ghosting, breadcrumbing e situationship. Le esperienze vissute sembrano inoltre lasciare una maggiore prudenza nei rapporti successivi: il 24% degli intervistati afferma di essere diventato più cauto o guardingo nei confronti di nuovi partner, mentre il 19% dice di avere maggiore difficoltà a fidarsi di una nuova persona.
Tra le fasce più giovani il fenomeno appare ancora più marcato. Nella fascia tra i 18 e i 24 anni, ad esempio, il 35% racconta di aver vissuto episodi di ghosting e il 32% una situationship.
Quando una frequentazione diventa difficile da decifrare
Di fronte a una situazione sentimentale poco chiara, la reazione più frequente indicata dagli intervistati è prendere le distanze: lo fa il 18%. Il 15% pensa invece che l'altra persona abbia perso interesse, mentre il 13% si chiede se abbia fatto qualcosa di sbagliato.
Sul piano emotivo, il 17% dichiara di tendere a distaccarsi, mentre il 14% prova a comunicare apertamente con l'altra persona per ottenere maggiore chiarezza. Il 12% preferisce concentrarsi sul lavoro o sui propri obiettivi personali.
La ricerca evidenzia anche alcune differenze tra uomini e donne. Le donne dichiarano più frequentemente di aver sperimentato ghosting, con una percentuale del 21% contro il 15% degli uomini, e riportano più spesso ansia durante una frequentazione, 14% contro 11%.
Maturità emotiva e paura dell'impegno tra le possibili cause
Agli intervistati è stato chiesto anche di indicare quali possano essere, secondo loro, le ragioni alla base di questi comportamenti. La risposta più frequente è la scarsa maturità emotiva, indicata dal 27%, seguita dalla paura dell'impegno, al 23%. Al 18%, a pari merito, vengono indicate la paura del confronto e delle conversazioni difficili e una cultura dei social media che favorirebbe forme di comunicazione a basso impegno. Solo il 12% indica invece nelle app di incontri la causa principale.
Secondo Corena Pezzella, Clinical Manager di Unobravo, nelle situazioni di maggiore incertezza può essere utile partire dal riconoscimento dei propri bisogni e comunicarli con chiarezza, cercando di distinguere tra la normale incertezza delle prime fasi di una frequentazione e dinamiche che meritano maggiore attenzione.
La ricerca restituisce così un quadro articolato del dating contemporaneo, nel quale accanto a nuove forme di relazione e di connessione emergono anche esperienze che possono rendere più difficile interpretare le intenzioni dell'altra persona. E, almeno per quanto riguarda il love bombing, Messina si colloca ai vertici della classifica tra le città considerate dallo studio.

È il "love bombing", una delle dinamiche analizzate in una nuova ricerca di Unobravo sul modo in cui gli italiani vivono il dating contemporaneo. E Messina spicca tra le città prese in esame.

Secondo i dati diffusi dalla società di psicologia online, il 24% dei messinesi dichiara di aver vissuto un'esperienza riconducibile al love bombing. title: Chase Infiniti on TIFF Breakout ‘The Julia Set,’ Love Bombing and Music Video Stardom
author: Matt Donnelly
body:
“The Julia Set” has emerged as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival.
In her feature debut, writer-director Niki Byrne crafted a perfect showcase for the talents of “One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti. The latter has earned raves for her turn as a math genius stuck under the thumb of an abusive boyfriend (and an academic system designed to ignore and exploit her).
“Julia’s off-the-charts intelligence, which Infiniti embodies with exquisite conviction, changes the stakes of the movie; we’re rooting for her emotional salvation, but we’re also rooting for her to dazzle the universe with her talent,” wrote Variety’s Owen Gleiberman in his TIFF review.
Indeed, Infiniti’s wide-eyed portrait of a prodigy is equal parts inspired and frustrating. Julia is recruited by a study group drilling for the Putnam Test — a six-hour math competition for undergraduates considered the most prestigious in the world. When Julia’s teacher’s assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney), comes on hard and fast with romantic feelings, we watch Infiniti’s Julia struggle to balance blossoming romance with the obligation she has to her extraordinary gifts.
Variety caught up with Byrne and Infiniti on the ground in Toronto this week, where the film premiered and is currently shopping for distribution
Niki, you’ve had an interesting trajectory. You were an aerial photographer and a licensed race car driver. How did we get to writer-director?
Popular on Variety
Niki Byrne: Everything I’ve done makes sense in reverse. I came back to California from Europe in 2018 and started working in L.A. I was writing quite a bit at that point, and I knew I wanted to write and direct. I took Martin Scorsese’s master class, where he said that if you’re going to be a director of any quality, you must take acting classes. So, I did and found it super valuable. I’ve worked in almost every department on a film set and found acting incredibly difficult.
Why?
NB: When acting is done poorly, it’s the easiest job on set. When it’s done well, it’s by far the hardest. I wrote this movie during [COVID] lockdown and came out with this sort of weird confessional script and linked arms with [my producers], and we went on the hunt for our Julia. Then this one walked into a coffee shop in Koreatown.
Chase, how long ago was that?
	Chase Infiniti: Three years ago. I was a month into shooting “Presumed Innocent.”
And you did “One Battle After Another” between then and now, crazy. One of the things that struck me about this performance is how restrained your character is – even in the face of serious abuse and mistreatment from people and systems.
	
CI: Well, it was a gift getting to bring Niki’s work to the screen. I was instantly drawn to it because Julia is a wonderful human being. It felt like telling a very real story that feels central to growing up. I had a Pascal, of sorts, [in my own life]. Everyone has. I remember a point in time where I was about 18, trying to figure out who I was and scared to show the world my talent. It’s hard to allow yourself to do that.
I think a lot of people might say that math is the antithesis of artistic work. How much did you have to engage with actual math problems?
CI: I had to pull from my own experience and flip it in a way that worked for what Julia was going through. I am not a math genius! Math is not my forte. I picked something else in my life that I felt I performed strongly at. I used that to build my confidence with math in the movie.
	And what was that thing you pulled from?
CI: I think I’m pretty good at my job. I thought about how I feel about performing in general and used that to create Julia’s energy behind her math skills.
Another thing that struck me about this film is that it’s one of the clearest examples of “love bombing” I’ve ever seen. There’s a scene where Julia is Pascal a surprise dinner at this apartment, using a key he gave her, and reacts as though she’s robbing the place.
NB: There were a lot of tears on set that night. Of all the moments we shot, the crew was gently sobbing during that one. We did multiple takes, and he would come in and be so unkind to her, and then she’d break and we’d all be gutted.
It’s also an important red flag that Pascal is capable of some monstrous things. Chase, not only is your Julia very retreating about her talent – she’s a socioeconomic underdog at her school and a woman of color. How does that inform the character in relation to her wealthy white boyfriend?
CI: Julia is always doing the next best thing for herself, and also for Pascal. Unfortunately, women of color don’t have the luxury of thinking only about themselves. They’re thinking for everyone around them. This is especially [true] in an abusive relationship. Women of color are some of the most unprotected people in society.
I have to pivot and ask you about your newfound music video stardom. You were amazing in the Ateez video for “Bad.”
CI: I just absolutely love them so much. Niki has heard so much about it. The first time we met, I told her she had to listen to them. I made her listen to “Ice on My Teeth.”
You know everyone’s going to want you to do a musical now that we’ve seen you sing and dance.
CI: I mean – I would love to sing and dance in a musical.

title: Best FWB Dating Sites Top 8 Picks Ranked for Online Dating
author: Amanda Grace; Levitated Media
body:
Surveys show 71% of daters have tried a friends with benefits arrangement, proof that casual dating without commitment has gone mainstream. FWB dating sites exist precisely because mainstream apps are built for long-term romance, not for members seeking NSA dating, local singles, or discreet casual encounters with intention matching from the first message.
This guide ranks the 8 best fwb dating sites and apps for privacy, geolocation matching, and genuine no strings attached connections.
Top 8 FWB Dating Sites & Apps
- AdultFriendFinder – Best Overall for Casual Dating and Community Size
- Ashley Madison – Best for Discreet, Anonymous Arrangements
- Meet-n-hook – Best for Fast Casual Meetups
- One Night Friend – Best for NSA Dating and Local Singles
- Tinder – Best Swipe Matching Dating App
- Bumble – Best for Women-Led Messaging
- Scruff – Best LGBTQ+ Dating Community
- OK Cupid – Best Free Registration for Intention Matching
Best Friends with Benefits Dating Platforms, Reviewed
AdultFriendFinder – Best Overall for Casual Dating and Community Size
AdultFriendFinder ranks among the largest adult dating platforms worldwide, with millions of active profiles spanning a broad, open-minded community. The site caters to casual dating, hookup arrangements, and friends with benefits connections across a wide range of orientations and relationship styles. Its scale and long operating history make it a default starting point for users exploring NSA dating online.
Key Features
- Geolocation matching surfaces nearby members for faster casual meetups
- Live chat, video calls, and cam features support real-time connection before meeting
- Free registration with basic browsing; premium membership unlocks full messaging
- Mobile app available for continuous access across devices
Pros
- Massive, active community with high daily engagement
- Inclusive of diverse orientations and relationship preferences
- Multiple communication tools beyond basic messaging
Cons
- Pricing details require digging beyond the homepage, so first-time visitors should check the membership page directly
- Explicit content runs throughout the platform, which suits members already comfortable with that format
- Verification efforts keep improving, though active users should still confirm details before meeting anyone new
Verdict
AdultFriendFinder suits users prioritizing community size and communication variety over a minimalist interface. It works best for open-minded individuals comfortable with explicit content who want fast access to local singles. Anyone seeking volume and flexibility in casual dating will find this platform difficult to match.
Ashley Madison — Best for Discreet, Anonymous Arrangements
Ashley Madison built its reputation on privacy first, casual dating second. The platform skips the public-profile model most dating apps use and instead runs on masked photos, untraceable billing, and a messaging system that never syncs to your other accounts. For anyone treating a friends with benefits search as something between them and no one else, this is the platform built around that exact need.
Key Features
- Photo masking blurs your image until you approve specific viewers
- Discreet billing shows a generic charge name on statements
- Panic button closes the app instantly and redirects to a neutral page
- Traveling Man feature flags members visiting your city short-term
Pros
- Privacy tools go further than most mainstream dating apps
- Billing discretion protects users worried about shared accounts or devices
- Traveling Man feature works well for local singles wanting low-commitment meetups
Cons
- Smaller day-to-day messaging volume compared to bigger platforms, better suited to patient users
- Premium credits add up fast for members who message often, so heavy users get the most value per dollar spent
Verdict
Ashley Madison suits members who rank discreet dating above community size. The privacy architecture is the actual product here, not an add-on, and it shows in every corner of the interface.
Meet-n-hook — Best for Fast Casual Meetups
Meet-n-hook strips out the profile-building rituals other platforms lean on. Sign-up takes minutes, and the matching algorithm prioritizes proximity and availability over long bios. This is a platform for people who want casual encounters arranged the same day, not a slow-build courtship.
Key Features
- Same-day matching surfaces active users within a set radius
- Simplified profile fields cut sign-up time to under three minutes
- In-app chat opens immediately after a mutual match, no waiting period
- Availability status lets members flag when they’re free to meet
Pros
- Fastest onboarding of any platform in this list
- Availability status filters out members who aren’t actually free right now
- Lightweight app runs smoothly even on older phones
Cons
- Smaller user base than the major dating apps, which rewards members in higher-density areas most
- Fewer filtering options than platforms built for detailed intention matching, so it works best for users who already know what they want
Verdict
Meet-n-hook earns its spot for speed. If profile depth and personality quizzes aren’t the point of your search, this cuts straight to who’s around and free tonight.
One Night Friend — Best for NSA Dating and Local Singles
One Night Friend leans hard into geolocation matching, surfacing local singles within a few miles rather than a whole metro area. The layout keeps things simple: a map view, distance filters, and profiles built around one question — what are you looking for tonight.
Key Features
- Map-based interface shows nearby members by exact distance
- Intention tags let users flag NSA dating versus ongoing arrangements upfront
- Free browsing with credit-based messaging for direct contact
- Mobile-optimized layout built for on-the-go use
Pros
- Map view makes local singles easy to spot without endless scrolling
- Intention tags cut down on mismatched expectations before the first message
- Credit system means you only pay for messages you actually send
Cons
- Credit-based messaging costs more per conversation than flat monthly plans, which favors members who message selectively
- Profile depth is thin compared to platforms built around long-term matching, since the format prioritizes speed over detail
Verdict
One Night Friend delivers exactly what the name promises. The map-first design and upfront intention tags make it a strong pick for anyone prioritizing local singles over a wide search radius.
Tinder — Best Swipe Matching Dating App
Tinder needs no introduction, and that name recognition translates into the largest active user base on this list. The swipe format keeps browsing fast, and the sheer volume of profiles means geolocation matching rarely comes up empty, even in smaller cities.
Key Features
- Swipe-based matching processes profiles faster than list-based browsing
- Super Like and Boost features increase visibility for active users
- Passport feature unlocks matching in other cities before you travel
- Free tier includes unlimited swiping with capped daily likes
Pros
- Massive user base means local singles are rarely in short supply
- Passport feature is genuinely useful for planning ahead in new cities
- Free tier is functional enough to test the app before paying for anything
Cons
- Broad user base includes people looking for everything from casual dating to long-term relationships, so intention matching takes more filtering on your end
- Premium features are gated behind multiple subscription tiers, which rewards users who commit to one plan rather than sampling
Verdict
Tinder wins on reach. If community size and geolocation matching options are the priority over precise intention filters, this is the safest default pick.
Bumble — Best for Women-Led Messaging
Bumble flips the standard messaging order: women send the first message in matches between men and women, with a 24-hour window before the match expires. That single rule changes the tone of the whole platform and cuts down on unsolicited messages significantly.
Key Features
- Women-first messaging rule structures every heterosexual match
- 24-hour match expiration encourages faster follow-through
- Bumble BFF and Bizz modes exist alongside the dating mode
- Video chat built directly into the app for pre-meetup screening
Pros
- Women-first messaging cuts down on unwanted contact significantly
- Built-in video chat adds a screening layer before agreeing to meet
- Match expiration keeps conversations from going stale
Cons
- The 24-hour window adds pressure for members with unpredictable schedules, which rewards users who check the app daily
- Same-sex matches don’t follow the women-first rule, so the core feature applies unevenly across match types
Verdict

title: Why relationship advice still needs human conversation
author: Jake Cole
body:
This article has been reviewed by a Digital Journal editor and may be licensed for reuse.
Artificial intelligence is moving into parts of life that once depended almost entirely on human conversation. A 2026 Marriage.com survey of 1,000 married U.S. adults found that 44% had used an AI tool for relationship advice. Separately, a September 2026 Elon University survey found that 27% of internet-using U.S. adults use AI for personal, emotional, or social interactions, a category that included relationship advice and romantic conversations.
Those figures do not necessarily suggest that chatbots are replacing counselors or partners. They may simply show that some people are turning to AI to think through conflict, uncertainty, or difficult emotions. Its accessibility may be part of the appeal, although relationship issues can involve perspectives and context that AI cannot fully capture.
Relationship questions can be particularly difficult for automated systems because the information they receive is usually limited to what one person chooses to provide. A response may therefore reflect only part of a disagreement, without access to the other person’s intentions, experiences, or interpretation of the same situation.
That limitation may matter when people use AI to interpret a partner’s words or decide how to respond to conflict. General guidance can offer another perspective, but relationship decisions often depend on context, communication, and an understanding of both people involved.
Sheila J. Simpson, executive director of FOCCUS Marriage Ministries, believes that convenience deserves to be separated from judgment. Her concern is not that couples use technology, but that they may give it a role that belongs more appropriately to direct conversation or qualified human support. “AI can offer immediate access when someone wants to think through a question,” she explains. “But I believe that convenience should complement, rather than replace, the perspective and understanding that can come from human relationships.”
The organization’s FOCCUS Pre-Marriage Inventory can be completed online, with the results used to generate reports that support subsequent discussion between the couple and a trained facilitator. The process then returns to guided human conversation. Simpson sees that sequence as important because a report can organize information, while a person can help two partners explore what those responses mean in the context of their own relationship.
“We only take technology to a point, and then we recognize that there has to be human intervention and discussion,” Simpson says. “Every relationship is unique. So, every solution must fit those unique circumstances.”
That becomes especially relevant when one partner asks an AI system to interpret an argument. The prompt usually reflects one person’s memory, wording, assumptions, and emotional state. The other partner is not present to clarify what they intended or how they experienced the same moment.
Simpson believes that limitations can be easy to overlook when an AI system feels highly personalized. “AI can’t read minds,” she notes. “You’re asking AI the question based on your assumptions to begin with, because that other person is not part of that discussion.”
Recent research gives that concern additional context. A 2026 study examining 11 AI models found that sycophantic responses, meaning responses that excessively affirm a user, could increase users’ confidence that they were right while reducing their willingness to repair interpersonal conflict. Simpson notes that the findings do not mean every chatbot response will reinforce one side, but they illustrate why agreement can be a weak substitute for understanding.
This also brings psychological safety into the conversation. Both people need enough space to express themselves honestly, clarify what they mean, and feel that their perspective has been heard. “Relationships are shaped by different histories, cultures, goals, habits, and expectations,” she explains. “Advice can offer a useful starting point, but it still has to be considered in the context of the two people involved.”
That does not leave AI without a constructive role. Simpson sees value in using it to identify resources, terminology, or types of professional support that someone may not know exist. “AI may be most useful when it helps someone identify the right professional resource,” she explains. “Rather than replacing expert guidance, it can help direct people toward qualified professionals who are better placed to support them.”
That distinction may become more important as AI becomes easier to consult. A chatbot can help someone organize a question or identify possible sources of support, but Simpson believes it should not take the place of direct communication between partners. “AI may help someone think through what they want to ask,” she explains. “But when the issue involves the relationship itself, I believe the next step should be to bring that conversation back to the two people involved.”
AI may help people organize their thoughts or find support, but Simpson believes the most important conversations should remain between the people in the relationship. As these tools become easier to use, the goal should be to support communication, not replace it.

title: "Les gens cherchent plus un emploi que la formation" : des candidats de tous âges en quête de nouvelles opportunités professionnelles au speed dating de l’emploi
author: Lucas MASSOT
body:
"Les gens cherchent plus un emploi que la formation" : des candidats de tous âges en quête de nouvelles opportunités professionnelles au speed dating de l’emploi
Le speed dating de l’emploi, organisé ce mardi à l’espace Cazot à Alès, attire un public varié, allant des jeunes en quête de premier emploi aux seniors en reconversion. L’événement permet aux entreprises et organismes de formation de rencontrer directement les candidats, offrant des opportunités du CAP au BTS dans divers secteurs.
C’était le défi proposé par le réseau Territoire, emploi, solidarité alésienne (Tesa). Un speed dating de l’emploi organisé ce mardi à l’espace Cazot, à Alès (Gard), qui ne rassemble pas que des jeunes à la recherche d’un premier emploi ou d’une formation. Sur place, des parcours variés, avec des candidats venus chercher un poste, mais aussi des pistes pour la suite de leur vie professionnelle.
"On arrive à recruter des candidats", explique Ludo Lombardi de L & B Coaching, alors que le rendez-vous permet aux entreprises et aux organismes de formation d’échanger directement avec les personnes présentes. Un public qui, selon Céline Ringot de CFA-Ecole Cévenole, est "divers, de tout âge". L’occasion de présenter des formations "du CAP au BTS", notamment dans différents secteurs professionnels.
Des profils divers
Parmi les visiteurs, une femme de 60 ans était notamment venue pour "chercher des idées" et pouvoir "se projeter". Un profil qui illustre une autre réalité de la recherche d’emploi : celle de personnes qui, après plusieurs années de vie professionnelle, cherchent elles aussi une nouvelle direction.
À lire aussi : "Faciliter la rencontre entre demandeurs d’emploi et entreprises… " : un grand job dating attendu à Alès pour la rentrée
"Les gens cherchent plus un emploi que la formation", observe par ailleurs Valérie, pour la Chambre de Métiers et de l’Artisanat du Gard. Mais derrière cette recherche, les situations restent différentes : certains veulent travailler rapidement, d’autres se renseignent avant de choisir une formation ou d’envisager une reconversion.
Pour autant, le monde des métiers manuels ne semble cesser d’attirer les habitants du Bassin, qu’ils soient en sortie d’étude ou en reconversion professionnelle. "Et sur ça, l’Intelligence artificielle ne nous remplacera jamais", sourit Céline Ringot.

title: Speed Dating con la scienza
body:
Cinque minuti per innamorarsi della ricerca! Mettiti comodo, scegli il tuo tavolo e preparati a un faccia a faccia ravvicinato con la scienza. Gli Speed Dating con la Scienza sono incontri lampo dove curiosità e scoperta si fondono: nessuna lezione accademica, solo il racconto vivo di chi esplora il nostro pianeta ogni giorno. Il tempo scorre, le domande corrono… tu a quale tavolo ti siederai?
1) Vulcani nel mondo e in Italia: un viaggio tra i vulcani d’Italia e del mondo per raccontare come la ricerca

title: Pan-African Girls’ Movement: Over 1,000 Girls To Benefit
body:
Pan-African Girls’ Movement: Over 1,000 Girls To Benefit
- Par LIENGU ETAKA ESONG
- 15 Sep 2026 13:12
- 0 Likes
The launching ceremony took place on Friday September 11, 2026.
A n initiative seeking to empo wer adolescent girls with knowledge, skills and confi dence to take control of their lives has been launched in Cameroon for the first time. The Pan-African Ado lescent Girls Movement, sponsored by the Graça Machel Trust and imple mented in Cameroon by Women for a Change Cameroon, was officially launched on Friday, September 11. The initiative targets adolescent girls aged 10 to 19 and young wo men between 20 and 26. It seeks to equip them with the tools to deve lop their talents, challenge social, economic and political norms that constrain their development and be come active contributors to their communities. During the launching ceremony on Friday September 11, the Pro gramme Officer for Adolescent Girls’ Movement at the Graça Machel Trust in South Africa, Dalrée de Lange, said the programme is built on the prin ciple that girls should be at the cen tre of decisions affecting their lives. “The programme came from the ado lescent girls themselves. They were the ones who said they wanted so mething for themselves”, she explai ned. Cameroon becomes the 15th African country to host the move ment, which already has “nests” in 14 countries. The expansion is ex pected to strengthen the initiative’s presence in Central Africa, particu larly in communities affected by conflict and other vulnerabilities. The movement hopes to be present in 16 African countries by the end of 2026. She further revealed that the programme covers issues including sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender-based violence, HIV and AIDS, teenage pregnancy, early marriage and menstrual hygiene. Participants will equally receive trai ning in entrepreneurship, leadership, education, climate change, food se curity, conflict resolution, policy change and advocacy. In Cameroon, the pilot phase is ex pected to reach more than 1,000 girls by December 2026. title: Read An Excerpt From 'Meet Cute Magic' by Morgan Elizabeth | The Nerd Daily
author: Elise Dumpleton
body:
A cozy cute enemies-to-lovers witchy fantasy for readers of Sydney J. Shields’ The Honey Witch and Sarah Beth Durst’s The Spellshop.
Intrigued? Read on to discover the synopsis and an excerpt from Meet Cute Magic by Morgan Elizabeth, which is out now.
She’s a witch who can’t fall in love without getting her heart broken. He holds a grudge like no other.
Bookstore owner Rosie Mayfield wants a love of her own, but it’s not meant to be––because of her family’s curse. To break it, she conjures a ghost who will break her curse, but for a cost––she has to brew a potion to help him transition to the other side. The problem? There’s only one person who hates Rosie in all of Heartwood Hollow, and she needs his help to complete the required task.
Jack Haggerty, the ghost’s grandson, has lamented about Rosie for years––she’s a disaster and she’s forbidden from visiting his gaming shop. He doesn’t believe in ghosts, so he’s stunned when his beloved grandfather makes an appearance. While he loves his family and will do anything to help his grandpa, he fights against the chemistry brewing between him and Rosie until he can’t anymore. But he doesn’t know how to tell her he no longer wants to go through with the plan, and she won’t admit that she’s falling for him because they’re doomed from the start.
